title: Mad respect to game devs
author: ParkInsider
selftext:
I work in enterprise software so not a dev, but I do design software customizations and I just recently started to hobby on a few game ideas through Claude.

Holy fuck guys. Making games is so much more difficult than doing my job.

When you make enterprise software, it:

1. Doesn't need to appeal to the user
2. Doesn't need to be fun
3. Doesn't need to make sense to anyone other than the user's boss

It's sooooo much harder to make a game, holy cow. I was working on this very simple game (a Bills Must Be Paid clone) for the past few weeks and it's about as good as anything I'm ever gonna make, easily 10x better than any customizations I've created in my 10-year career, and it still friggin' sucks compared to millions of free games you can find.

So yeah, just wanted to tip my hat to indie game devs. To have to make the look, sound, feel, mechanics, loops, progression, lore and any of the other dozen of other extremely important aspects, have to fit in a cohesive package is incredible. Being a hobbyist at this makes me appreciate how crazy it is that Stardew Village is a thing, how TF did rollercoaster tycoon ever came to life... 

Respect.

comments.author: CandidateDue2480
comments.body:
The first 80% is the easiest part too, the last 20% is typically referred to as "the last 80%" 😆

Most devs dont actually speak out much against AI. Most of us are using it, or have to use it.

For a lot of devs this "revolution " is no different than the last tools upgrades. Many people will swarm in, but few will finish. 

Its always nice to see who survives the waves, because they become part of the community and we all get better for it.

It'll be a while yet before the waves calm.

comments.author: witmann_pl
comments.body: Yup. I do enterprise webdev and it's easy as pie compared to game dev. Not even close.

comments.author: Briskfall
comments.body:
Dev teams that got big backlash then managed to turn it around like No Man Sky's are impressive. I would have been boomed and not have the mental resilience, lol.

When solo-ing, it's like having to fill in the shoes (the plates) of so many roles. One would think that it's just about "to ship" a game but the constant communication and PR, that feels immensely draining, haha...

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
Like any other job, the paycheck helps, I'd imagine.  People like to think of game dev as this wild, scrappy place full of passion but for a lot of those guys software development is software development and they're getting paid six figures to write code whether the game bombs or is a smash hit success.  Especially given how much of it is contract work - they're getting let go after launch either way, or were simply hired to write more code to unfuck the disastrous launch.  

Lot of it simply gets outsourced too.

comments.author: Excellent-Basket-825
comments.body:
I make both. It's not, both is incredibly hard on it's own. Enterprise applications are complex due to differen things and since you have to satisfy different stakelholders.

It's a different discipiline to optimize for efficiency vs. fun. A lot of game devs could learn \*a lot\* from classical software development and validation practices. I'm not even sure whether most have ever talked to actual people other than their friends when they were testing their games.

The people who comment that work in enterprise are mixing up the comparison of a simple slice of a function vs. the whole discipline. Making enterprise software \*alone\* is equally as hard as making a game \*alone\*. It's fucking tough as nails because it's very very very complex in a lot of different ways.

It's "easier" to be a game dev in a big team where you're assigned a specific role, in both roles.

replies.author: Correct_Emotion8437
replies.body: Another enterprise dev here.  I would say that enterprise software does need to appeal to the user, it does need to make sense and the user experience, while not “fun” is really important.   Id also say that except for the art, there are more similarities than differences between enterprise and game coding.

comments.author: bigorangemachine
comments.body: As someone who went for college for digital art and is now a dev with 20 years XP .... People don't know how to animate. Drives me crazy... Time to goal not seconds of animation....

replies.author: shesaysImdone
replies.body:
> Time to goal not seconds of animation

I'm confused by this

replies.author: bigorangemachine
replies.body:
I forget the proper word

Basically when you animate stuff you will say "3s" but something happens in the UI and it only needs to animate half as much (opacity is 40 instead of 100). The animation is now feeling slower because the 3s was based on 100 opacity. But now it's 3s for 40 opacity 

So you need to figure out the goal "current to 0 opacity" against your expectation "100 opacity to 0 in 3s"

Previously I wrote "pixels per second" but that was worse.... Because you aren't always dealing in pixels

comments.author: SpanielsAreBest
comments.body: Started as an indie game dev, went to college, entered business, got a contract at a game studio for smartphone games for a phone that was coming to market, went back to business software, left industry due to disability, and now I am back to writing games. Honestly, while the game studio I was with had some of the most intelligent people I ever met, they were also some of the least smart programmers I ever met when it came to things like building scale-able software or designing network communications. Game development has always been more about who you know and who you are friends with, and having seen the inside of a fairly big studio, i chose to go back to business software. Way less drama and the hours were better than some bullshit "crunch time" schedule. I am way more excited about game development than I have been for years now.

replies.author: Bavariasnaps
replies.body: couldnt we ask AI to write our games in assembly and make the super efficient?

replies.author: ConsistentAnalysis35
replies.body:
It wouldn't be anything more super efficient than AOT and JIT compilers can output. The "super efficiency" of ASM starts when you do handwritten optimizations by an expert low-level engineer, and AI isn't really going to give you those, even if you prompt it "You are an expert low-level engineer".

To that point, you can do handwritten optimizations in Java and get absolutely bonkers performance almost as good as in unmanaged languages. But that is a task far more difficult than just vibecoding your shit.

replies.author: Jacmac_
replies.body: I think you could do it by specifying that the application must be written in Assembly. However, it would likely be very time/token consuming for the agent(s) to test and debug. There is also not too much up to date documentation compared to the mountains of documentation for other languages, it's like the AI would be using the specifications from Intel and AMD as a guide.

replies.author: Kindly_Life_947
replies.body: yes but performance is more than assembly. To be efficient you would have to write your own tools and framework.

replies.author: GoalAnxious7288
replies.body: that's insane... never knew that. true legendary stuff

replies.author: Jacmac_
replies.body: Parts of Quake were written in Assembly, Michael Abrash was a sort of legendary Assembly programmer, and he was coaxed into leaving Microsoft for Id for a stint to work on Quake. His books were really great. Back in the 80s-90s, a lot of the really good games or applications had a fair bit of Assembly for specific use cases.

comments.author: Shrineheart
comments.body:
As a solo dev? Thank you. Folks really don't get just how much work goes into a game even if you use AI to assist. I've had a lot of my game in mind for years and I've been learning from YouTube and articles about level design, researching what players want from the genre, etc that whole time.
I actually spent a lot of time reading about what other devs would do different if they started over too.
Stardew is amazing and Concerned Ape did a hell of a job on it.
Also man, Rolercoaster Tycoon has mechanics that are more in depth than I remotely thought. On YouTube there's a vid by I think it's small indie dev and juniper dev that just dives into how the nausea and puke system works in Roller Coaster Tycoon. Someone sat down and planned out a whole mechanic around how that worked. I played the heck out of that game as a kid and it feels wild seeing stuff like that now.

comments.author: BasilKey8088
comments.body: This is why the anti AI game dev mob makes no sense to me. I wouldn't say it's as difficult as my dissertation or a few of the more complex jobs I've held yet but even making a vertical 2d phone game is absurdly difficult and time consuming as a solo dev using AI. I have dozens of game design docs, multiple pipelines like art and audio I've put together, etc. I don't even have a playable copy yet after hundreds of hours. The mob assumes we just ask a chatbot to make a clone of an existing game but tweak one thing then just wait around snorting glue for a few minutes or hours. There is a complete disconnect because they mostly just use AI for free therapy sessions or cheating on homework.
